issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff in a title-based suit governed by the former limitation regime who admits dispossession or ouster bears the burden of proving possession within the limitation period.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership through a court auction purchaser and sought partition and possession of a share of the house.
The plaint alleged that the defendants asserted ownership, prevented tenants from paying rent to the plaintiff, and obstructed the plaintiff from managing the house and collecting rent.
The defendants pleaded that they had been in adverse possession for more than twelve years.
The plaintiff's own allegations therefore amounted to an admission of dispossession or ouster.
issues.conclusion: The plaint disclosed an admitted dispossession or ouster, so the plaintiff had to prove actual or constructive possession within twelve years; the burden did not shift to the defendants merely because they were co-sharers.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, as applicable to the case, a title-based plaintiff who admits dispossession must establish possession within twelve years. Section 3 required the court to determine whether the suit was within time. The Court relied on Bindhyachal Chand v. Ram Gharib Chand for the distinction between the burdens under Articles 142 and 144, and distinguished Manikyala Rao v. Narasimhaswami because the pleadings there did not admit dispossession and symbolic possession there interrupted adverse possession within the relevant period. The Court noted that the 1963 Act clarified the position but did not decide the law under that Act.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking possession or partition on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.former_limitation_framework: The suit was governed by the former limitation regime applicable to title-based possession claims.
predicates.plaintiff_admitted_dispossession_or_oust: The plaintiff's pleadings acknowledged that another person had excluded the plaintiff from possession or denied the plaintiff's rights in a way amounting to ouster.

issues.definition: When a title-based possession suit is governed by the former limitation framework and the plaintiff's pleadings admit dispossession or ouster, the plaintiff must establish possession within the limitation period.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding a title-based possession suit must determine whether the plaintiff had actual or constructive possession within the limitation period, and the absence of that finding requires the decree to be set aside and the case remitted for determination.
material_facts: The auction purchaser had received symbolic possession, but Kripa Shanker continued to occupy the house.

The plaintiff alleged that the auction purchaser had possessed the relevant share with the other co-owner, while also alleging that the defendants prevented rent from being paid to the plaintiff and obstructed the plaintiff's management of the house.
The symbolic possession relied on in the proceedings had occurred more than twelve years before the suit was filed.
Neither the trial court nor the appellate courts made a finding on whether the plaintiff had actual or constructive possession within twelve years of filing suit.
The record could be considered by the first appellate court, the final court of fact, to determine the possession issue.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the judgments and orders of the High Court and first appellate court were set aside, and the case was remanded to the first appellate court to determine from the evidence whether the plaintiff had actual or constructive possession within twelve years of filing suit. Receipt of rent or other evidence could establish constructive possession; if the plaintiff established timely possession the suit was to be decreed, and otherwise it was to fail.
issues.legal_principle: For a claim governed by Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908, proof of actual possession is not essential if the plaintiff establishes constructive possession within twelve years, including through receipt of rent or otherwise. A court must make a finding on that crucial question. Where the lower courts have not made it, the final court of fact may be directed to determine it on the evidence already on record.

predicates.appeal_from_possession_decree: A party appealed from a decree granting possession or partition in a title-based possession dispute.
predicates.timely_possession_finding_absent: The lower courts did not determine whether the plaintiff had actual or constructive possession within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.evidence_on_record_available: Evidence already on the record could be assessed by the court entrusted with determining the disputed possession issue.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a possession decree presents an absent finding on timely possession and evidence is available, the decree is set aside and the case is remanded for that determination.
